- If sentiment is positive (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ 0.33) or flat, model often underestimates downside risk; add buffer or adjust downward bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply decay or lagged mean reversion to dampen forecast.
- Model consistently overpredicts early in the 30-day horizon when sentiment is neutral or mildly positive — adjust for horizon bias by reducing initial forecast values.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 85), model fails to recognize it — apply downward correction if sentiment is weak or neutral.
- If sentiment history shows increasing positivity (e.g., 0.33 → 1.00), model may overreact — cap forecast growth rate to avoid overcorrection.
- For sentiment history with repeated 0.33 or 0.67, model often underestimates volatility — increase forecast variance or add stochastic adjustment.
